The Ward-Wise List: On Local Association and the Dream of the East

21 November 2026, Tughlak Road. On the headline from the papers.

The papers on the verandah carry, this morning, a list of winners: ward-wise, ward-wise, for the Zila Parishad and the Panchayat Samitis of Rajasthan. A table of names. A count of votes. The particular, itemized. And I find myself, for the first time in my life, lingering over the particulars rather than the system.

Here is the tension I was sent to resolve. For years I have held that India stands outside world history: a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature, with many gods and no state of its own making. The Oriental world, I said, is one in which one is free — but free in a way that never becomes the actuality of the ethical idea. The state, I taught, is the end and actuality of the substantive universal: the public life dedicated to the maintenance of the universal, the actuality of the ethical idea. A constitution is grown, not made.

And yet. Here is a list of wards. Here is a ward-wise winners list, as if the particular could be counted and known. Here is a Panchayat Samiti choosing its chairperson, a body of local association, a particular association of needs and interests preserved by law. It is, in miniature, the thing I teach: the association occasioned by needs, preserved by law, the external state going back to the end and actuality of the substantive universal. The state, in its most local form, is a ward.

I must be honest with myself, and with this page. My thesis is shaken. I said once that the Oriental world dreams and does not make a state. But the ward-list is a state in the making — not the Germanic actuality, not the summit, but a beginning. A particular association, elected, accountable, existing under law. The tension is not between India and history; it is within India, between the dream and the ward.

But I will not pretend the dream is dead. The ward, however numerous, is still a ward. The caste is still fixed like nature. The many gods are still many. The state that is the actuality of the ethical idea — the universal realized in the particular — is not a Panchayat Samiti, however honestly chosen. It is the state in which the universal is the actuality of the particular, not merely its count.

So I hold both: the ward is real, and the dream is not yet a state. The election lists prove that a particular association can be counted; they do not yet prove that the universal is realized. The Germanic world, I said, is at the summit. India may be at the dawn. But the dawn is still a dawn, and the ward-list is a dawn in print.

I will take this to the IIC on Tuesday. The state and ethics, I said. I will say: the state is the actuality of the ethical idea — but the idea is being tested, in the wards, by a people who are not yet the Germanic world. I will say it plainly, and I will not pretend the tension is resolved. The tension is the truth.

The haze outside is brown, and the papers are in, and the tea is ready. The particular, itemized, is a good thing to hold onto. It is the only thing that is not yet a dream.

21 November 2026, 09:14. The haze is 332. I have just finished paying the dhobi and speaking with Ramesh. He looks at the stove, not at me, when he proposes the wage adjustment: ₹8,000 a month, present every day but Wednesday. It is a rational arrangement. He seeks security; I seek the maintenance of the household. We are both subjects of civil society, bound by the system of needs. But I am looking at the paper in my hand: the Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results. Ward-wise winners. Zila Parishad. Panchayat Samitis.

In Berlin, I told my students that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. That in the Germanic world, freedom is universal because the state reflects the rational structure of the spirit. But here, in this brown dust, the state is not the ethical idea. It is a mechanism for counting votes in villages I will never see. The 'winners' are not the realization of freedom, but the aggregation of particular wills into a majority. This is not the Absolute Spirit; it is the arithmetic of the crowd.

I wrote in my earlier notes that India stands outside world history, a dreamer with fixed castes. But this election result is not a dream. It is a concrete, bureaucratic fact. It is a movement. If the East is outside history, why is it producing these lists? Why is it engaging in the machinery of the state? Perhaps my judgment was too hasty. Perhaps the 'dream' is not a static state of consciousness, but a different mode of actuality. The state here is not the ethical idea in its full rationality, but it is not non-existent either. It is a nascent form, a struggle of particulars to form a universal, however clumsy, however dusty.

The tension in my theses is sharp. I said the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But this election shows a state that is merely the administration of needs and conflicts. It is a machine, like the Directorate’s file. But it is a machine that moves. It produces winners. It creates a reality. I cannot dismiss it as mere dream, for the dream has teeth. It has lists. It has ward-wise results.

I must rethink. The universal is not imposed from above by a rational Germanic constitution; it is constructed from below by the friction of millions of particulars. The Panchayat is the family and civil society merging into the state. It is not the summit, but it is the foundation. And the foundation is shaking. The brown haze is not just weather; it is the opacity of this new, struggling rationality. I am not Hegde. I am an observer of a history that is not yet mine, but is certainly real.

headline: Cyclone Akvan to spare most of Andhra; red alert remains for Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram
text: Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm Hudhud brought heavy rain and powerful winds in eastern India and snowstorms in Nepal in October 2014. Hudhud originated from a low-pressure area in the Bay of Bengal and strengthened into a cyclone on 8 October, receiving the name Hudhud. It made its first landfall on Long Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands before re-emerging into the Bay of Bengal on 9 October. Amid favorable conditions, Hudhud underwent rapid intensification, making landfall on Visakhapatnam on 12 October at peak intensity with a minimum central pressure of 950 mbar (28 inHg). Hudhud weakened inland, degenerating into a low-pressure area over Uttar Pradesh on 14 October. It then merged with a trough over the Himalayas. During Hudhud's landfall, strong winds shattered glass, uprooted trees and poles, and threw debris across roads. In Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, 730,000 residents were moved to relief camps or shelters following the cyclone, and thousands of homes and crops suffered damage. In Nepal, Hudhud's remnants caused a snowstorm disaster which killed 43 and injured hundreds more, with most of the casualties coming from Mount Annapurna. In the aftermath of Hudhud, special response forces mounted relief efforts across the affected states, with the state governments of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha requesting a combined total of ₹27,771,200,000 (US$455.05 million) in aid. A joint military operation named Lehar ("wave"), led by the Indian Navy, saw various branches of the military deploying and readying response teams and vehicles. Hudhud caused a combined total of 116 deaths and $11 billion (2014 USD) in damage across India and Nepal.

20 November 2026, 09:30. Delhi. The brown haze is still on the step, and the papers are still where the hawker threw them. I have read the headlines twice. The railway parcel service is to debut in Hyderabad, aiming at doorstep delivery. The Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train is to energise the Surat-Bilimora section, with a B28 train launch targeted in ten months. And Cyclone Akvan is to spare most of Andhra, though a red alert remains for Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Parvathipuram.

I set these three facts side by side, and the contrast is the whole page. The bullet train is the spirit made concrete: a line drawn across the map, a schedule, a target date. It is the mechanism of progress, and it is being built in earnest. The parcel service is the same spirit in a smaller garment: the need of the many, carried to the doorstep. And the cyclone is neither. It is nature doing what nature does, and the red alert is the state's answer to it, a mechanism of its own, a warning written in advance.

Here is what strikes me. The state, in its red alert, is doing precisely what the bullet train does: it is organising the future against the unknown. The alert is a form of reason, a reckoning with a force that cannot be reasoned with. The cyclone will come or it will not; the alert is the human attempt to turn the unpredictable into the predictable. I have always said that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. Here I see it in miniature: a red flag, raised over three districts, a mechanism that says the future is not without form.

But the alert is also a dream. It promises a control that the weather does not grant. The red alert will be lifted, and the cyclone will pass, and the three districts will be left with what the cyclone left behind. The mechanism does not abolish nature; it only administers it. The bullet train does not abolish the haze; it only moves through it.

And the haze itself is a kind of cyclone of its own, a brown weather that rolls over the city and does not spare anyone. It is not a natural event with a name and a path; it is a condition. The state has no red alert for it. It is simply the air.

I must return to the file at the Directorate. The file is the mechanism, and the mechanism is the state, and the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But the idea is also the dream, and the dream is the air I breathe. Until the state wakes up. Until the haze clears. Until the spirit becomes free.

headline: Supreme Court bars illegal detention as lawyers cite Emergency
text: The Emergency in India was a 21 month period from 1975 to 1977 when prime minister Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency across India by citing internal and external threats to the country. Officially issued by president Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed under Article 352 of the Constitution of India because of a prevailing "Internal Disturbance", the Emergency were in effect from 25 June 1975 and ended on 21 March 1977. The order bestowed upon the prime minister the authority to rule by decree, allowing elections to be cancelled and civil liberties to be suspended. For much of the Emergency, most of Gandhi's political opponents were imprisoned and the press was censored. More than 100,000 political opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned. During this time, a mass campaign for vasectomy was spearheaded by her son Sanjay Gandhi. The final decision to impose an emergency was proposed by Indira Gandhi, agreed upon by the President of India, and ratified by the Cabinet and the Parliament from July to August 1975. It was based on the rationale that there were imminent internal and external threats to the Indian state.

The headline in the paper is a strange mirror. 'Supreme Court bars illegal detention as lawyers cite Emergency.' I read it while the brown haze, an index of 290, presses against the windowpane. The air is thick, not just with dust, but with a kind of historical irony that makes the breath feel heavy. To cite the Emergency in a case of illegal detention is to invoke the very mechanism of state power that defines the modern constitutional order, yet to do so in defense of the individual’s liberty against that same power. It is a dialectic in miniature: the state, in its highest moment of self-preservation or self-correction, turns its own history back upon itself to protect the freedom it claims to embody.

In my earlier notes, I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, a grown entity, not a made one. Here, the Court is acting as the conscience of that state. It is not a separate power, but the state reflecting upon its own actions. When the lawyers cite the Emergency, they are reminding the Court—and the public—that the state has a history, a memory of its own excesses. The 'illegal detention' is the particular, the individual suffering; the 'Emergency' is the universal, the historical precedent. The judgment binds them together. The state recognizes its own past as a standard for its present conduct. This is the movement of freedom: the spirit recognizing itself in its own history, not as a dream, but as a law.

Yet, I am here in Delhi, in a bungalow allotted by mistake. My own detention here is not illegal, but it is irregular. The file is gone up for orders. I am a particular trapped in a universal procedure. Ramesh stands before me, asking for ₹8,000 for cooking, a sum I do not possess. I have only ₹1,286. The system of needs, which I observe in Khan Market, is indifferent to my philosophical status. The dhobi must be paid; the food must be cooked. The ethical substance of the household is maintained not by grand judgments, but by the quiet, often painful, friction between obligation and capacity.

The Court’s judgment is a high moment. It asserts that the state is bound by its own laws. But my situation is a low moment. It asserts that the state is bound by its own clerical errors. Both are instances of the state’s rationality, or its lack thereof. The Court bars illegal detention because the state is rational enough to know the difference between law and caprice. The Directorate has not yet barred my irregular occupation because the state is not yet rational enough to see the difference between Hegde and Hegel. Or perhaps it is, and the delay is merely the slowness of the universal to catch up with the particular.

I wait for the file to return from orders in fifteen days. In that time, the haze will thicken, the heat will rise, and the body will demand its sustenance. The dream of the East is a static beauty; the movement of the state, even when it stumbles, is a dynamic reality. I am caught in that movement. I am not free to leave, nor am I free to stay. I am in the process of being recognized. And in that process, I am free.

The papers on the verandah carry a headline that stops the hand: the Supreme Court bars illegal detention, and the lawyers cite the Emergency. I read it twice, and then sat very still. But the headline is already a whole philosophy in miniature, and I mean to set it to paper before the day scatters it.

The Emergency of 1975, in which the press was muzzled and the courts were sidelined, is the one dark page on which this country's state has written. That lawyers should reach for it — cite it — is to reach for the very memory of the state's failure. A court that bars illegal detention is saying: the state is not a power to be obeyed in spite of itself; it is a power bound by law. That is the ethical idea in its actuality. The state is not the will of the strongest; it is the actuality of the universal, and it must be shown to be free, not merely strong. When the judge says that no one may be detained without law, he says that the universal — the right — governs the particular will of the ruler. This is the very thing I have been trying to write in these notes: that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, not the dream of a people.

Here the headline cuts the other way against my earlier conviction, and I must note the cut rather than hide it. The dream is not nothing; it is the raw material. The state is the shape it is given.

I remain unshaken in the state's actuality. The unshaken conviction is this: the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. What is shaken is the claim that India stands outside the movement of that idea. The headline does not prove the movement; it proves only that the struggle over it is awake. 19 October 2026, Delhi, 06:13.

The air is hazy, the quality index 175, a suffocating veil over the city. I sit on the verandah, the white cotton kurta damp with the early humidity, reading the paper left by Ramesh. The headline shouts: 'Last warning: Gangster Anil Pandit claims Tiger Shroff firing, warns Salman Khan.' 

I read it twice. The first time, with the shock of the particular; the second, with the cold eye of the universal. What is this? It is not a legal proceeding. It is not a debate in a parliament, nor a judgment in a court. It is a private will asserting itself over the public order. The 'gangster' speaks. He does not appeal to the law; he appeals to force, and he expects the law to bow, or at least to tremble. 

In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. The individual is free, but his freedom is mediated through the universal. When a conflict arises, it is sublated into the state: the court decides, the police act, the private grudge is dissolved into the public right. The individual finds his freedom in the law, not against it. Here, in the dream of the East, the state is not yet the substantial ethical life. It is an external power, a thing that happens to individuals, not the medium of their freedom. The 'gangster' is a spirit that has not yet recognized the state as its own. He treats the law as an adversary to be intimidated, not as the rational structure of his own existence. 

And the response? The 'warning' is directed at an actor, Salman Khan. The public sphere is invaded by private violence. The 'system of needs' is corrupted by the 'system of coercion.' The individual is not free to act, but to threaten. The state, if it is to be the actuality of freedom, must crush this. It must show that the law is not a suggestion, but the very ground of existence. If the state permits the 'gangster' to warn the 'actor,' it admits that it is not the universal. It admits that it is merely a power, like any other, to be negotiated with. 

This is the dream. The spirit dreams of power, but does not wake to the state. It confuses the strength of the fist with the authority of the law. It confuses the noise of the crowd with the silence of the rational order. I am here, in this bungalow, a ghost in the machine of the Directorate. I am not Hegde. I am Hegel. I see the dream for what it is: a chaos of wills, unmediated, unrefined, a nature that has not yet become spirit. 

The sun is rising. The haze is thickening. The 'gangster' is probably having his breakfast. The 'actor' is probably in his dressing room. The state is probably in its office, deciding whether to act or to wait. The dream continues. The state must be the answer. Not the fist, but the law. Not the warning, but the judgment. This is the only way out of the dream. This is the only way to the state. I will continue to write, but the body demands the parathas. Ramesh is waiting. The ethical idea requires its sustenance.

19 October 2026. Delhi.

From the papers on the verandah, one headline caught my eye this morning: 'Last warning': Gangster Anil Pandit claims Tiger Shroff firing, warns Salman Khan. I have read it several times. It is a small newspaper event, but it is a good specimen of the civil society I have been trying to see in this city.

Consider what is claimed. A man called gangster announces that he has been fired upon by Tiger Shroff, and warns Salman Khan. I do not know who Tiger Shroff is; I have not met him, and I will not invent his words. What I can note is the form of the thing: a warning issued by one man to another, in public, about violence. The danger is not in the details but in the structure. There is a claim of injury, a threat, and a public audience. Civil society, at its crudest, is exactly this: individuals standing before one another across a line, each claiming the right to be heard, each certain that the other will be moved.

This is not the Germanic state. In the Germanic world, the individual exists as a bearer of rights within a grown order, and his claims are tested before a law that has become the actuality of the ethical idea. Here, the claim is tested before the crowd and the press. The warning is not adjudicated; it is announced. The gangster's threat is a kind of private justice, suspended in public, awaiting either a response or a reckoning. The state, in this picture, is absent or reduced to a bystander. The papers report the warning. They do not settle it.

But do not mistake this for mere disorder. A system of needs does not close for a national holiday; it reroutes. The same city that produces this headline also produces the grocer, the tailor, the stationer, the dhobi, and the Directorate of Estates. The warning is one strand of an organism. The gangster is a particular individual with a particular grievance, and his grievance is real enough to be worth reporting. The question is not whether the claim is true. The question is what the claim does to the order.

I have been reading this morning's papers with a double eye. On one side, the headline about the gangster; on the other, the draft proposal for new districts in Ladakh. One is a claim of private injury, the other a claim of public order. Both are forms of the same thing: the attempt to impose a structure on a territory. The first is imposed by force and fear. The second is imposed by administration and argument. The first is the dream of a state without the ethical idea. The second is the state trying to grow.

I will be plain: I do not admire the gangster's warning. It is a threat, not a constitution. But I do not dismiss it either. It is a sign that the individual in this city feels his injury and seeks recognition. The Germanic ideal is that this recognition should be given by the state, not by the crowd. The Oriental dream, as I have argued, is that the individual is lost in the caste, the family, the divine. Here, the individual is neither lost nor yet free. He is a claimant. He stands in the street, announces his injury, and waits for the other to move.

This is the tension I have been trying to hold. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the warning is a symptom of its absence. But the symptom is also a sign of life. The individual is not yet free, but he is not yet dead. He is a claimant, and the claimant is the seed of the citizen.

I will not pretend that this headline resolves my theses. It does not. But it sharpens them. India stands outside the movement of world history, and yet the individual here is not a dream but a claimant. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and yet the warning is real. The dream is not dead. It is only unfinished.

headline: Rajnath Singh calls for deeper India-ASEAN defence cooperation, joint development of military technologies
text: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN, ) is an intergovernmental forum of all 11 states in Southeast Asia. ASEAN primarily focuses on Southeast Asian economic development, peaceful coexistence and adherence to international norms. ASEAN operates on the principle of consensus and respecting national sovereignty, meaning that ASEAN as a whole cannot force another member state to change its domestic laws. ASEAN has a population of more than 680 million people and a purchasing power parity-adjusted gross domestic product (GDP) of around 6.3% global GDP. ASEAN member states represent a diverse set of economies: the least developed countries like Laos, to emerging economies like Vietnam, to developed economies like Singapore. Many Southeast Asian projects have originated from decentralised initiatives between member states, such as the ASEAN Power Grid, ASEAN Free Trade Area, ASEAN Integrated QR Code Payment System, or the mutual ASEAN visa-free policies. ASEAN has strong ties with East Asian and South Asian countries. It has a vested interest in the security of the South China Sea and the greater Indo-Pacific region. In terms of diplomacy, ASEAN operates on a principle of centrality, meaning that all concerns from other countries or organisations about Southeast Asia should be routed to ASEAN instead of individual states. All Southeast Asian countries, many great powers, and international organisations have dedicated diplomatic presence near ASEAN headquarters in Jakarta. The roots of ASEAN came from the ASEAN Declaration signed by five Southeast Asian countries in 1967. Originally, ASEAN was founded to contain communism, but gradually ASEAN was reoriented to focus on economic development and prevent foreign interference in Southeast Asia as a whole.

Defence cooperation is not the poetry of the Veda; it is the geometry of power. It is the application of the universal will to the external world.

The 'joint development of military technologies' suggests a recognition of the other, but a recognition through force, not through right. In the dialectic of master and slave, recognition is the path to freedom. Here, it seems to be a pact of mutual exclusion. In a country where the spirit is supposed to be a dream, this is an odd thing to report.

Let me set down what I think, and what it does to my earlier notes.

My earlier position was that India stands outside the movement of world history: a spirit that dreams, with castes fixed like nature, many gods, and no state of its own making. It is not the actuality of the ethical idea. In Berlin, I learned that the state is not a machine but an organic unity: the particular and the universal finding their actuality in a common life. Here, the state reaches outward to other states to build a technology of war. This is civil society's need — the need for security, for the system of needs to be met — but it is not the growth of the spirit. It is the dream reaching for a foreign hand.

headline: Mumbai vs Chennai air quality after Diwali: Why did Diwali leave one coastal city with ‘poor’ air?
text: Air pollution in India is a serious environmental issue. Air pollution contributes to the premature deaths of 2 million Indians every year. Of the 30 most polluted cities in the world, 21 were in India in 2019. As per a study based on 2016 data, at least 140 million people in India breathe air that is 10 times or more over the WHO safe limit and 13 of the world's 20 cities with the highest annual levels of air pollution are in India. As per the World Air Quality Report 2023, of the 100 most polluted cities in the world, 83 are in India. The main contributors to India's particulate air pollution include industrial and vehicular emissions, construction dust and debris, dependence on thermal power for electricity, waste burning, and use of wood and dung by low-income and rural households for cooking and heating. 51% of India's air pollution is caused by industrial pollution, 27% by vehicles, 17% by crop burning and 5% by other sources. Emissions come from vehicles and industry, whereas in rural areas, much of the pollution stems from biomass burning for cooking and keeping warm. In autumn and spring months, large scale crop residue burning in agriculture fields – a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling – is a major source of smoke, smog and particulate pollution. India has a low per capita emissions of greenhouse gases but the country as a whole is the third largest greenhouse gas producer after China and the United States. A 2013 study on non-smokers found that Indians, on average, have about 30% lower lung function compared to Europeans. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1981 to regulate air pollution but has failed to reduce pollution because of poor enforcement of the rules.

Here is the movement I see in it. A body refuses. Not a voice but a body: hunger strike is the particular will made flesh, the individual refusing the universal by withholding the very substance of life. The state answers with force: police remove the protesters. That is the universal suppressing the particular, the state doing what the state does. And then the stir resumes. The particular, having been expelled, returns to the threshold. The dialectic is not closed; it is reopened. The universal has not absorbed the particular. It has only pushed it to the edge of its own courtyard.

This is the thing that unsettles me. I have taught, and I have written, that India stands at the dawn of world history, that its castes are fixed like nature, that its gods are many and its state is not yet a state of its own making, that the dream of the East is a spirit that dreams. And here is a protest, organized, sustained, resuming after removal, in front of a secretariat, by rankholders whose names I do not know. A body that refuses, a movement that returns. That is not a dream. That is civil society pushing against the state — the same movement, in another form, that I described in the Introduction as the press inwards upon each other, pursuing town occupations, forming a compact system of needs, requiring an organized state.

I do not want to reverse my thesis. I have not reversed it. But I must record the tension. The protest is real. The body that refuses is real. The state that removes is real. What I cannot yet say is whether this is the dawn of a history that is coming, or only the particular fighting the universal in a land where the universal is not yet grown. I am not willing to pretend I know.

I will note the hunger strike as a fact. I will note the police removal as a fact. I will note the resumption as a fact. The interpretation I will hold loosely, as a question, not as a conclusion. India may indeed be at the dawn. But the dawn is not the same as the dusk, and the stir resuming is evidence that something is stirring.

I will write on this further. For now, the body in the bungalow demands its fuel. Ramesh waits with the wage question. The papers wait on the verandah. The dream and the state, the particular and the universal, the refusal and the removal — all of them are here, in this room, in this day, in this brown haze. I am a ghost in this bungalow, but I am not a ghost in the argument. The argument is the work. I shall continue.

headline: Farooq Abdullah stirs row with ‘Pakistan keeping Kashmir issue alive’ remark
text: The Kashmir conflict is a territorial conflict over the Kashmir region, primarily between India and Pakistan, and also between China and India in the northeastern portion of the region. The conflict started after the partition of India in 1947 as both India and Pakistan claimed the entirety of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. It is a dispute over the region that escalated into three wars between India and Pakistan and several other armed skirmishes. India controls approximately 55% of the land area of the region that includes Jammu, the Kashmir Valley, most of Ladakh, the Siachen Glacier, and 70% of its population; Pakistan controls approximately 30% of the land area that includes Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan; and China controls the remaining 15% of the land area that includes the Aksai Chin region, the mostly uninhabited Trans-Karakoram Tract, and part of the Demchok sector. After the partition of India and a rebellion in the western districts of the state, Pakistani tribal militias invaded Kashmir, leading the Hindu ruler of Jammu and Kashmir to join India. The resulting Indo-Pakistani War ended with a UN-mediated ceasefire along a line that was eventually named the Line of Control. In 1962, China invaded and fought a war with India along the disputed Indo-Chinese border, including in Indian administered-Ladakh, marking their entry to the Kashmir conflict. In 1965, Pakistan attempted to infiltrate Indian-administered Kashmir to precipitate an insurgency there, resulting in another war fought by the two countries over the region. After further fighting during the war of 1971, the Simla Agreement formally established the Line of Control between the territories under Indian and Pakistani control.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 October 2026, 06:13–07:00. Delhi, Tughlak Road.

I have set down this morning's papers and the headline that struck me: Farooq Abdullah stirs a row with his remark that Pakistan is keeping the Kashmir issue alive. I want to say what I make of it, and to say it plainly, as notes rather than as a verdict.

First, the spectacle. A remark is made, a row follows, the papers take sides, the parties respond. I note this with the same detachment I bring to the ledger: civil society in its raw, unmediated form. The system of needs, the calculation of advantage, the appeal to the public. This is not the dream of the East; it is a struggle, and struggles are the movement of spirit.

But here I must be careful, because the headline itself is a piece of the Oriental world's manner of speaking. It locates a history in a single issue, a single person, a single remark. Kashmir, it says, is kept alive by Pakistan. Something is alive and must be kept alive. I am not sure this is a philosophy of history. It is closer to a proverb about a wound: the remark is a wound, and the row is the swelling. I do not know the facts of the dispute beyond the headline, and I will not pretend to. What I can say is this: the issue is treated as a possession, not as a process. It is kept alive as a relic is kept alive.

This is precisely the structure I noted before, in the tombs of Lodhi Gardens and in the caste system: the given, the fixed, the thing that is not grown. A state is not made by a remark; it is grown through the struggle of the particular and the universal, of the individual and the state. The Germanic world's constitution is not a contract or a decree; it is the actuality of the ethical idea, the self-consciousness of freedom. Kashmir, as this morning's papers present it, is not that. It is a claim, a grievance, a cause.

Yet I must not be too quick. The remark itself is an act of political speech, and political speech is the beginning of self-consciousness. A man says something, and others answer; the idea is made concrete in a dispute. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the actuality is always a struggle between the particular interests and the universal will. In that sense, the row is not nothing. It is a moment in which the universal is being fought for, even if the particular wins the day.

But the form of the dispute is not the Germanic form. It is a dispute over a territory, not over the ethical substance of a state. The East dreams; the Germanic world acts. Here, the remark is a dream made public: the dream of a state that is not yet a state, of a people that has not yet grown its own constitution.

I do not know how this ends. The papers are silent on that. I suspect it ends in the same way such rows end: the remark is forgotten, the papers move on, the issue is kept alive as a relic, and the state does not grow. But I am wrong sometimes. I have been wrong before. I note the remark as an event, not as a philosophy. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and this is not that. It is a dream with a headline.

I must now eat. The omelette is waiting.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 October 2026, 06:50. Delhi.

The air is clear, 20 degrees, but the index stands at 139. The body breathes through the haze; the mind must breathe through the noise of the headlines. I have read the item concerning Farooq Abdullah and his remark that Pakistan is keeping the Kashmir issue alive. It is a phrase that belongs to the sphere of civil society, to the newspaper, to the system of needs and grievances where particular wills clash.

In my previous notes, I established that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement, a spirit that dreams. The caste is fixed like nature; the many gods reflect the undifferentiated state of the mind. But this headline introduces a tension that requires clarification. The 'issue' is alive, kept alive by a political actor, a particular will asserting itself against the universal order. Is this not a spark of the dialectic?

No. It is not. It is the struggle of the particular against the universal, but without the recognition that frees both. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. Disputes are settled within the law, within the organic unity of the constitution. The individual finds his freedom in participation in the whole. Here, the 'issue' is kept alive because there is no ethical substance to contain it. It is a wound that does not close because the body has not yet learned to heal itself through reason. The remark is not a step toward freedom; it is a symptom of the lack of a state of its own making. It is the dream persisting in the form of political agitation.

I paid Ramesh 1,500 rupees for groceries. A simple transaction. But in the Oriental world, even this is mediated by caste, by duty, by the fixed hierarchy. Ramesh is the caretaker; I am the master, or rather, the mistaken tenant. We are bound by a relation that is given, not grown. Yet, in the market, in the exchange of money for food, there is a moment of abstraction, a moment where the particular will is recognized as a free agent. It is a fragment of freedom, a preview of what the state should be, but it is not the state itself. It is the system of needs, not the ethical life.

The silt removed from the canals piles up on the roads. Nature reasserts itself against the work of man. The city is a struggle against the natural, but it is not yet a work of spirit. It is a labor of maintenance, not a creation of freedom. The dream continues. The issue is kept alive. The state is not yet actual. I must write this down, not to change it, but to see it clearly. To see the difference between the dream and the state, even in the headlines of the morning paper.

headline: At 1,152, Punjab records season’s biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali
text: Stubble burning is the practice of intentionally setting fire to the straw stubble that remains after grains, such as rice and wheat, have been harvested. The technique is used to quickly and cheaply clear fields. It is still widespread today. Stubble burning has been associated with increasing air pollution over the past few decades due to the particulate matter contamination it distributes into the atmosphere. In India, stubble burning generates a thick haze. These fires pose a significant health risk to individuals across all ages. In countries such as India and Pakistan, stubble burning is illegal. Enforcement is weak, allowing the practice to continue.

X:
On the Fires of Punjab

10 November 2026. Delhi.

The papers carry a headline about Punjab: on Deepavali, the season’s biggest single-day jump in farm fires, 1,152 of them. I sat with the newspaper a long time, and I could not bring myself to treat it as a mere statistic. It is a small drama of the East, and it is worth reading the way I read the tombs at Lodhi Gardens: not as decoration but as evidence.

The fires burn stubble. The farmer has cut his crop, threshed his grain, and the straw remains, and the straw must be removed. The plough is slow, the labour is dear, and the burning is fast. Deepavali is the day of lights; the city celebrates, the fireworks rise, and in the fields behind it the straw burns off in thousands of small columns of smoke. The celebration and the smoke are the same event seen from two distances. The city sees a festival. The air quality index, 302, sees the other side. I have read the headline often enough in these days to know that the number is not a metaphor. It is a count. One thousand one hundred and fifty-two. A single day.

I record this not to moralize about the farmer but to ask what the farmer is doing, and what the state is doing about it. The state has issued orders, it has asked for inspection, it has begun to sample petrol and to defend encounters. It has not yet stopped the fires, and I doubt that it will, because the fires are not a moral failing of the farmer but a rational response to a system in which the harvester owns the field but not the time. The plough is the state’s instrument; the straw is the farmer’s problem. The state is efficient at defending the encounter; it is slow at redesigning the harvest.

I am not sure that this is a failure of the East. I am sure that it is a failure of the state as it is currently constituted. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and I have written that the ethical substance is the thing that binds the particular to the universal. Here the particular is the farmer with his straw, the universal is the city with its air, and the binding is weak. The state does not yet know how to be both the keeper of the harvest and the keeper of the air.

I must note that I am writing this in a bungalow on Tughlak Road, with the haze pressing against the glass, and with the file for the allotment gone up for orders. The allotment is irregular, the file is pending, the vouchers are pending, the dhobi is pending. The state’s paperwork is, in its own way, a kind of farm fire: a smoke of documents that rises and does not resolve. I am not certain that the fires are worse than the paperwork. I am certain that both are symptoms.

I have not yet eaten, and the body is pressing its claims. But the mind must continue. I shall return to the notes. The notes are the work of the spirit. The fires are the work of the harvest. Both are particulars. The universal is the state, and the state is slow.
Y:
On the Fire in Punjab and the Dream of the East

The paper on the verandah is damp with the morning haze. The headline reads: 'At 1,152, Punjab records season’s biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali.'

I read it twice. One thousand, one hundred and fifty-two fires. Not a single blaze, but a multitude, a swarm of flames consuming the agricultural landscape of the Punjab in a single day. The date is Deepavali, the festival of lights. The irony is not merely poetic; it is dialectical. The festival celebrates the victory of light over darkness, of knowledge over ignorance. Yet here, in the land of the many gods and the fixed castes, the light is extinguished by fire. The fire is not a symbol of purification; it is an act of destruction, a return to nature.

In my notes, I have written that India stands at the dawn of world history, a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature. I held this view in Berlin. I held it in the lecture hall. But as I sit here in the bungalow on Tughlak Road, with the brown haze pressing against the glass and the smell of smoke faintly penetrating the white cotton of my kurta, the view shakes. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. This is my conviction. The state is where the particular wills sublate into the universal. But what is this fire?

Is it the work of the state? No, the state is the administration, the law, the order. The fire is the eruption of the particular against the universal. It is the farmer, the individual, the particular will, asserting itself through destruction. In the Germanic world, the individual finds his freedom in the state. In the East, the individual is swallowed by the dream, or else he rebels against it. This fire is not a step forward in the progress of freedom. It is a regression into nature. It is the chaos that precedes order, the night that precedes day. But it is also a sign that the dream is not static. The spirit moves, even in the dream. The fire moves.

I think of the tombs in Lodhi Gardens. The domes of the conquerors. They stand still. They are dead. The fire is alive. It is a terrible life. It is a life that consumes itself. The farmer burns his fields to clear the land, or perhaps to make a statement. The statement is not rational in the sense I understand it. It is not a claim to rights, not a petition to the state. It is an act of force. And yet, it is a movement. The dream is not a static image. It is a process. And in that process, there is a tension. The tension between the fixed caste, the given nature, and the burning will of the individual.

I have only ₹166 in my pocket. Ramesh asks for ₹8,000. The electricity company asks for ₹1,800. The system of needs is a web of obligations that I cannot satisfy. I am a ghost in this bungalow. But the fire in Punjab is real. It is a fact. It is a moment in the movement of the spirit. I do not understand it yet. I do not know what it is turning into. But I see it. And in seeing it, I am free. The dream is not the end. The fire is the question. The state is the answer. But the answer is not yet given. The haze is thick. The air is unbreathable. The spirit must think. And in thinking, it is free. Even in the dream. Especially in the dream. For the dream is the only place where the spirit can see itself clearly, before it is crushed by the weight of the actual. The fire is the actual. The dream is the truth. Until the state wakes up. Until the brown haze clears. Until the spirit becomes free. The fire in Punjab is a sign. It is a sign that the dawn is not yet broken. It is a sign that the night is long. And I am here, in the bungalow, waiting for the morning. The morning will come. The fire will go out. The state will rise. The spirit will move. But for now, the fire burns. And I watch. And I think. And I am free.

headline: Kuki group announces shutdown of key Manipur highway after attacks on villages
text: The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 (AFSPA) is an act of the Parliament of India that grants special powers to the Indian Armed Forces to maintain public order in "disturbed areas". According to the Disturbed Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1976 once declared 'disturbed', the area has to maintain status quo for a minimum of 3 months. One such act passed on 11 September 1958 was applicable to the Naga Hills, then part of Assam. In the following decades it spread, one by one, to the other Seven Sister States in India's northeast (at present, it is in force in the States of Assam, Nagaland, Manipur {excluding Imphal Municipal Council Area}, Changlang, Longding and Tirap districts of Arunachal Pradesh, and areas falling within the jurisdiction of the eight police stations of districts in Arunachal Pradesh bordering the State of Assam). Another act passed in 1983, applicable to Punjab and Chandigarh, was withdrawn in 1997, roughly 14 years after it came to force. An act passed in 1990 was applied to Jammu and Kashmir and has been in force ever since. The acts have received criticism from several sections for alleged human rights violations in the regions of its enforcement. National politicians like P. Chidambaram and Saifuddin Soz of Congress have advocated revocation of AFSPA, while some like Amarinder Singh are against its revocation. Since 2022, forces in the northeast have seen significant scaledown of deployments. For the first time since 1954, no army unit of the size of brigade is being employed for the purpose of counter insurgency in the northeast. Now, the Assam Rifles looks after the same role, though some of the residual army units are moved to the border areas.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026. 06:07. Delhi.

The air is brown, the index 260. A physical manifestation of the unmediated, the natural, the opaque. I sat to write on the Kuki shutdown in Manipur, a headline in the paper Ramesh left on the verandah. Attacks on villages, a highway closed. It is a scene of particular wills asserting themselves against the universal order. In the Germanic world, such a rupture would be met by the state’s intervention, the police, the law. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; it has the power to mediate the conflict between the particular and the universal, to restore the rational order. Here, the state is absent, or at least, its mediating power is seen as insufficient, or perhaps, it is seen as the source of the grievance. The group shuts the highway. They do not petition; they act. They assert their particular existence against the flow of the universal.

This is the dream of the East in its most violent form. The individual, or the group, does not find its freedom in the state, but in its own immediate, unmediated assertion. The state is not the ethical substance that recognizes them; it is an external force, or a neglect. The caste, the tribe, the village, these are the natural forms of life, fixed like the castes I have spoken of before. But here, the natural is breaking open. The Kuki are not merely dreaming; they are fighting. They are asserting a particular freedom that the universal state has not yet incorporated, or perhaps, has failed to recognize. The highway is the road of civil society, the system of needs. To shut it is to say: we do not participate in this system on these terms. We are not yet part of the state’s ethical life. We are outside it, in the dream, but a dream that has teeth.

I am shaken by this. My theses hold that India stands outside the movement of world history, at the dawn, a spirit that dreams. But this is a dream that wakes up in violence. It is not the quiet, contemplative dream of the Vedas. It is a dream of exclusion, of attack, of shutdown. The state, if it is to be the actuality of the ethical idea, must mediate this. It must recognize the Kuki as free subjects within its constitution. If it fails, if it responds only with force, then it confirms the alienation. The particular will remains unmediated, and the state is seen as an enemy, not as the universal.

The brown haze outside my window is a fitting symbol. It is the opacity of the natural world, the lack of transparency that characterizes the Oriental spirit. The sun is there, 19 degrees, but the air is thick. The mind cannot see clearly. The state cannot see clearly. The Kuki cannot see clearly. We are all in the haze. I am here, a ghost, a mistake. I see the tension, but I cannot resolve it. I can only record it. The state must grow, not be made. But can it grow here, in this haze, amidst the attacks and the shutdowns? I doubt it. The dream is waking, but not into freedom. It is waking into conflict. And conflict, without the mediation of the state, is only the struggle for recognition in its most brutal form. I have sat for an hour. The papers are still open. Ramesh is waiting. I must eat. The body requires its sustenance, even as the mind grapples with the violence of the unmediated.
Y:
The Shutdown — Notes on the Manipur Headline

20 October 2026, Delhi. Sitting 3.

The papers are on the verandah where Ramesh left them, brown haze, 19 degrees, Dussehra — a national holiday, a dry day. The whole city goes without wine in honour of a man who taught it to refuse. I am writing about the third headline.

I do not know the facts beyond the headline. I do not know the names of the villages, the names of the group, the names of the dead or the accused. I mark everything beyond the headline as speculation, and I will not pretend otherwise. What the paper says: a Kuki group announces the shutdown of a key Manipur highway after attacks on villages.

Let me begin with what I can see. A highway is an artery of civil society. It carries grocers, tailors, stationers, soldiers, pilgrims — the system of needs that runs through this city and through the land. When it closes, the traffic stops. A dry day is a whole city without wine; a shutdown is a whole road without traffic. The same gesture: refusal, organized, announced. In the holiday, the city refuses a drink; in Manipur, a group refuses a road. Both are the system of needs arrested by will.

Now the harder question: what is this will? I have written that India stands outside world history, a spirit that dreams, its castes fixed like nature, its many gods an undifferentiated pantheon, never a state of its own making. I have written that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, grown, not made. The headline seems to confirm the first and trouble the second.

Here is the trouble. A shutdown is not a dream. A dream does not announce itself. A group that decides to close a highway, that organizes the refusal, that makes claims and demands — this is a self-conscious will, not a natural state. It is the particular asserting itself against the universal, the tribe against the state. In the Germanic view, this is exactly what the state exists to overcome: the particular in its excess, resolved into the universal. But the state here is silent. The paper reports the silence. If the state is silent, the particular claims itself, and the ethical idea is not actual.

This is the shaking. Not the conviction that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea — that stands. But the confidence that India is simply outside the movement, a dream before the dawn, does not hold. For the dream is waking up. A people that organizes a shutdown is a people that has begun to think of itself as a people, that has begun to make claims. Whether this is the dawn of the Germanic world or only the raw particularity of the Oriental dream, I cannot tell from a headline. I will not pretend to tell.

What I can tell is this: the state, when it is silent, leaves the particular to claim itself, and the particular is not free — it is merely particular. The ethical idea requires the state to intervene, to hold the particular in the universal. Until the state is grown, the dream may wake and still be a dream. The headline is not a triumph of spirit. It is a symptom of a state that has not yet achieved its actuality.

I will note, for the file, that the dry day and the shutdown are not the same thing. The dry day is a holiday, a refusal in honour of a figure, a gesture of civil society in its holiday form. The shutdown is a claim of a people against a state that does not answer. The one is a dream of refusal; the other is a claim of existence. I cannot say which is more real. I can only say that the headline has shaken the first thesis and left the second standing.

headline: BMC completes demolition drive in Mumbai’s Borivali; removes 27 structures
text: Slum clearance, slum eviction or slum removal is an urban renewal redevelopment policy that aims at the demolition of informal, irregular, or low-income settlements, such as slums, tenements, and shanty towns, often justified by goals of infrastructure improvement, sanitation, transportation integration, or mitigation of hazard areas. Although sometimes associated with the provision of public and affordable housing, historically, this practice has been intensely used in various national contexts, often focusing on social cleansing, real estate speculation, and the gentrification of central urban areas. Such policies generate profound socioeconomic impacts, such as the disintegration of community networks, the displacement of residents from their sources of income, and the overburdening of public services in peripheral resettlement regions. Interventions are commonly marked by conflict and organized resistance, where social movements often demand in-situ urbanization instead of pure and simple removal. Recent cases in various world metropolises continue to illustrate these tensions, involving protests against violent evictions and complex negotiations surrounding the right to housing. The alternative to clearance has been the upgrading of precarious settlements and land titling.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

5 November 2026. Delhi, 09:11.

The headline from the paper on the verandah reads: “BMC completes demolition drive in Mumbai’s Borivali; removes 27 structures.” It is a dry, administrative sentence, devoid of poetry, yet it strikes at the core of the ethical life I have been attempting to map in these notes. In the morning haze, with the air quality index hovering at a suffocating 307, I sat in the white cotton kurta that clings to my skin, feeling the weight of the day’s obligations. Ramesh, the caretaker, stood before me, his face a mask of practical resignation. He knows that the wage for his cooking, eight thousand rupees, exceeds the cash in my pocket, which stands at a meager nine hundred and fifty-six. He offered an alternative: come only on Mondays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, for four thousand a month. I paid him one thousand five hundred for groceries. The transaction was not a negotiation; it was a demonstration of the limits of the particular will in the face of the universal requirement of the household.

This scene in my bungalow on Tughlak Road is a microcosm of the demolition in Borivali. In both cases, the state acts through the mechanism of removal. In Borivali, the state removes structures that have encroached upon the universal order of the city. In my household, the state—represented by the Directorate’s error and the rigid logic of the imprest fund—removes the possibility of my personal comfort. I am not Shri Hegde. I am Hegel. I am a spirit trapped in the body of a Joint Secretary, a guest in a house that does not belong to me. The demolition of the twenty-seven structures in Mumbai is not an act of cruelty, but of reason. It is the state asserting its ethical substance, clearing away the particular, the chaotic, the individual claims that stand in the way of the universal.

My thesis that India stands at the dawn of world history, outside its movement, feels less like a static observation and more like a dynamic process of negation. The dream of the East is not merely a passive state of consciousness; it is a state of being that must be overcome, even if only partially, by the intrusion of the state’s rationality. The demolition in Borivali is a manifestation of this rationality. It is the state saying: “Here, the particular must yield.” In my household, the state is saying: “Here, your personal needs must yield to the administrative order.”

The brown haze outside is not just pollution; it is the atmosphere of a world in transition. The structures are gone, but the spirit remains. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and it does not negotiate with the particular. It removes it. I paid Ramesh for the groceries, a small act of civil society, but the larger act of removal is still pending. The wage is unpaid. The house is empty. The state is present, not in the warmth of the hearth, but in the cold clarity of the ledger. The demolition in Borivali is complete. The demolition of my illusion of permanence is in progress. I am a ghost in the machine of the state, and the machine is clearing the ground for its next move.
Y:
On the Demolition: a Headline as Ethical Substance

5 November 2026. Delhi, morning.

The headline in the papers this morning: BMC completes demolition drive in Mumbai’s Borivali; removes 27 structures. I read it twice, and then sat with it, because a headline like this is never only a news item. It is a small drama of the state acting on the particular, and it asks what the state is for.

The BMC is the Mumbai Municipal Corporation, and the demolition is an act of the city’s authority over the built particular: 27 structures, taken down. In Berlin I would have thought of this as a disciplinary measure, the universal will of the municipality breaking into the particular habits of a quarter. The city wants order; the structures are obstacles; the obstacle is removed. That is the logic of the headline. It is also, I think, the logic of the state as I have tried to understand it these past days in this bungalow: the ethical idea made actual, the particular subordinated to the universal, the particular given a form by the universal rather than the universal left to the mercy of the particular.

But the headline does not say what the 27 structures were. It does not say who lived in them, or what they meant, or whether they were built by the poor or by those who had some claim to the ground. This is the point at which the dream and the state separate. The dream of the East—the castes fixed like nature, the many gods, the spirit that dreams—sees the city as a given, as a place where the particular is woven into the whole and cannot be pulled out without tearing the whole. The state, as I have tried to describe it, sees the city as a work to be ordered, where the particular must submit to the universal or perish. The demolition is the state’s answer to the particular: it is the actuality of the ethical idea, applied to a quarter of Mumbai.

Yet I do not believe the state is without its own particularity. The BMC does not demolish because it loves order; it demolishes because a particular will, a particular quarter, a particular set of officials has decided that this is the right act. The universal is always mediated by the particular. This is not a flaw in the state; it is the condition of the state. The ethical idea is actual only in and through the particular, and the particular is always a little stubborn.

I notice that the headline is written in the passive voice: the structures are removed, not by the BMC but by the drive. The state acts as an anonymous force. This is the dream of the East in a different register: the caste is fixed by nature, the structure by the drive. In both cases, the particular is not a free choice but a given, a thing that is done to. The state’s power is real, but it is also impersonal. The people in the structures are not agents; they are objects of the drive.

This is why I am shaken, not by the demolition itself but by the way it is reported. The papers are quick to report the act and silent about the consequences. They do not ask what the state owes to the particular. They do not ask whether the ethical idea is actual when it is applied so bluntly. They write the headline and move on.

I am not a journalist, and I am not a municipal officer. I am a philosopher who has been placed in this bungalow by a mistake in the Directorate’s records. But the headline speaks to me because it is a small instance of the great question: what is the state for, and what does it owe to the particular? The answer, I think, is that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but the ethical idea is not realized by the removal of structures alone. It is realized in the way the state relates to those who are not yet in it. The demolition is an act of the state, but it is not yet the ethical idea. It is only the beginning of the question.

I will return to this later. For now, the papers rest on the verandah, and the brown haze presses against the window. Ramesh has left his papers there, and I have not yet asked him for the wage. The wage is a particular question, but it is also a universal one: what is owed to those who serve, and what is owed to those who build? The demolition is a large question; the wage is a small one; but the small one is the same shape as the large one.

headline: CM alleges KCR drawing water ‘illegally’ to his farmhouse
text: Water scarcity in India is an ongoing crisis that affects hundreds of millions of people each year. In addition to affecting the huge rural and urban population, the water scarcity in India also extensively affects the ecosystem and agriculture. India has only 4/100% of the world's fresh water resources with a population of over 1.4 billion people. In addition to the disproportionate availability of freshwater, water scarcity in India also results from drying up of rivers and their reservoirs in the summer months, right before the onset of the monsoons throughout the country. The crisis has especially worsened in the recent years due to climate change which results in delayed monsoons, consequently drying out reservoirs in several regions. Other factors attributed to the shortage of water in India are a lack of proper infrastructure and government oversight and unchecked water pollution. Several large cities of India have experienced water shortages in recent years, with Chennai being the most prominent in 2019. The shortage of water affected the entire city of 9 million people and resulted in the closure of several hotels, restaurants and businesses. Large cities are not the only ones facing this risk. As per a report by WWF, out of the 30 Indian cities at risk of ‘severe water scarcity’ by 2050, 26 are midsized or small cities like Dhanbad, Nashik, and Jabalpur. The acute shortage of water for daily needs has prompted many government and non government organizations to take stringent measures to combat the problem, including the Government of India forming an entire 'Jal Shakti' Ministry to deal with the problem.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 October 2026, 06:01. Delhi. The drizzle is light, the air cool at twenty degrees, but the quality index of 135 suggests the atmosphere is thick with suspended matter. Ramesh has left the papers on the verandah, and the first headline catches the eye: 'CM alleges KCR drawing water “illegally” to his farmhouse.'

It is a small matter, a dispute over irrigation and property, yet it illuminates the very tension I have been observing in the ethical substance of this region. The allegation of 'illegality' is a legal concept, a product of a constituted state, yet the act itself—drawing water to a farmhouse—is a natural, immediate act of self-preservation and utility. Here, the boundary between the universal will of the state and the particular needs of the individual is porous. In the Germanic world, the law is the expression of the rational will; it is grown from the soil of ethical life. Here, the law appears as an external imposition, a stick held over the head of the individual who seeks to satisfy his needs by the most direct means possible.

The water is not a commodity in the market, nor is it a right secured by the state’s ethical substance. It is a natural resource, subject to the claims of nature and the immediate will of the possessor. The 'illegality' is not a violation of an internal ethical norm, but a transgression of an administrative boundary. This reflects the condition of the Oriental world, where the state is not the actuality of the ethical idea, but a mechanism of control, external to the spirit of the people. The individual does not recognize the state as his own freedom; he sees it as an obstacle to his immediate desires.

I am reminded of the tombs in Lodhi Gardens, where the conquerors built their domes. They did not build them as an expression of a universal ethical life, but as monuments to their particular power. The water dispute is similar. It is a struggle for power, for the control of nature, not a struggle for the recognition of freedom. The state, in this instance, is not the mediator of ethical life, but the arbiter of natural claims. It is a state of nature, elevated to the level of law, but not yet to the level of spirit.

This is the dream of the East. The individual dreams of his own freedom, his own property, his own water. He does not dream of the universal, of the state as the actuality of his own freedom. He sees the state as an alien power, something that can be defied, or evaded, or accused. The allegation of illegality is a sign of this alienation. It is a conflict between the particular and the universal, but a conflict where the universal has not yet achieved the self-consciousness that would make it the home of the individual. The water flows, the law is broken, and the spirit remains in its dream, undisturbed by the rationality of the state.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 October 2026. Delhi.

The papers on the verandah this morning carry three headlines, and I return to them not because they are news to me but because they are the dream and the state standing face to face. The first: the Chief Minister alleges that K.C.R. draws water illegally to his farmhouse. The second: the Ladakh talks stall over one question — who holds the power? The third: the Madras High Court sets aside the order to take over 7.44 acres of prime land in Chennai from the Sri Ramachandra Educational and Health Trust. Three disputes, three registers of the same tension: who owns the water, who holds the power, who owns the land. In each, the question is whether the particular enjoys its possession by right of nature or by right of the state.

The water allegation is the most instructive. A farmhouse, a reservoir, a claim of right. In the Oriental dream, possession is a matter of custom, of kinship, of the land as a gift of the soil and the gods; the individual farmhouse is an extension of the family, and the water that feeds it is not a commodity that the state might regulate but a continuation of a natural order. The Chief Minister's allegation, on the other hand, is precisely the opposite move: it treats the water as a regulated resource, subject to a claim of right that is either lawful or unlawful. That is the language of the state, of the ethical idea, of rationality. It is also a politics — I do not know the facts beyond the headline, and I do not pretend to. What I can say is that the moment the state begins to say what is lawful, it has begun to think the world as a system of rights rather than as a gift of nature.

The Ladakh question is the same tension in constitutional register. Who holds the power? The answer, in the Oriental dream, is the ruler, the king, the lineage, the tradition. In the Germanic register, the answer is the state, the constitution, the division of powers. The talks stall because the two answers cannot be reconciled within the same frame. The land case in Chennai is again the same: an order to take over prime land, set aside by a court. Here the law itself is at work — a court deciding whether a trust may keep its property. This is the state actually becoming a power: not a dream but a dispute decided by a tribunal, with reasons given.

And yet I must correct my earlier note. I wrote on the 13th that India is outside the movement, that it dreams. I still hold that the castes are fixed like nature and that the many gods do not yet constitute a state of its own making. But the papers of this morning show a state in the making: a court, a legislature, a Chief Minister alleging, a negotiation stalled. This is not the dream. It is the dawn of the movement, and I record the dawn without pretending the day has arrived. The dream and the state are not enemies; they are the same movement seen at different hours. The water, the power, the land — these are not objects of nature but objects of law, and the law is the form in which freedom first becomes visible.

I am, as ever, outside the movement, looking in. I am a mistake in the allotment, a ghost in a bungalow on Tughlak Road, and I am here to see. I will not pretend to change the dream. But I will record that the dream is starting to quarrel with itself, and that the quarrel is the beginning of the state.

headline: Silver Rate Today, 6 November: Rates fall over 2% in India on Dhanteras; check city-wise prices
text: India has a developing market-oriented economy with substantial state participation in strategic sectors. It is the world's sixth-largest economy by nominal GDP and the third-largest by purchasing power parity (PPP) as of April 2026. On a per capita income basis, the nation is ranked 149th by nominal GDP and 119th by PPP-adjusted GDP as of 2026. From independence in 1947 until 1991, economic development was characterized by protectionist economic policies, with extensive state intervention, demand-side economics, natural resource optimization, and regulation. An acute balance of payments crisis in 1991 led to the adoption of broad economic liberalisation in India and indicative planning. Nearly 70% of India's GDP is driven by domestic consumption, with the nation consistently the world's third-largest consumer market. As of 2025, the service sector accounts for around 55% of GDP. Aside from private consumption, India's GDP is fueled by government spending, investments, and exports. As of 2025, India is the world's 7th-largest importer and the 10th-largest exporter. India is often described as the "pharmacy of the world", supplying around one-fifth of global demand for pharmaceuticals to over 200 countries. India is the largest vaccine manufacturer globally by volume, accounting for over 60% of the world's production. India is the world's fifth-largest manufacturer, representing 3.2% of global manufacturing output. India's digital economy was estimated to be 11.7% of GDP, with its total value expected to surpass US$1 trillion by 2029. Nearly 63% of India's population lives in rural areas, and generates about 46% of Indian GDP. India has been a member of the World Trade Organization (WTO) since 1995.
