On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

21 October 2026, Delhi. Morning.

The papers lie on the step where the hawker threw them, and among their headlines one catches the eye better than the rest: “The ECI’s unfinished lessons.” I have read the other two with the amusement a man gives the newspaper: the guest lecturers to be paid more, announced in a budget that has not yet paid them; and the Secretary of State saying that the US-India deal is down to a few words, weeks from finalising, ninety-nine per cent done. These are the talk of a state that moves by speeches and contracts. But the third line, the ECI’s unfinished lessons, is the one that stays with me, because it is a sentence about the state itself, and it is a sentence that admits the state has not finished learning.

I must be honest about what the headline means, and I mark all interpretation here as interpretation. I do not know its source or its argument. I know only the words, and what they do to my mind. An unfinished lesson is a lesson not yet learned. The Election Commission, the institution that conducts the elections, is said to have lessons — lessons of its own history, presumably — that it has not finished. If that is right, then the state here is still in the pedagogical stage, and the pedagogy is not yet complete. That is a surprising phrase to apply to the state, and I apply it gladly, because it is the phrase my own history has taught me.

In Berlin I held that the constitution is grown, not made. Here I find a state that has been made, assembled from parts, amended, re-amended, and has yet to finish the lesson of its own making. The elections are the closest thing this land has to a moment of self-consciousness — a gathering of the particular into a whole, a choice among powers, a show of the universal will. But the unfinished lessons suggest that the choice does not yet become the ethical substance. The people vote; the state is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea. There is a gap between the ceremony of election and the life of the state. The lesson is unfinished because the state has not yet learned to be what it pretends to be.

This is, I confess, a reading, not a report. The papers do not tell me what the lessons are. They do not tell me what is unfinished. But the tension is real enough for me to work with: a state that conducts elections, that issues orders, that appoints commissions — and that has not yet finished learning what its own institutions are for.

I think of the vouchers pending before me, the dhobi due on Saturday, the imprest that wants to be paid back, the Directorate that allotted this bungalow to the wrong man. All of this is the state as an administration, a system of needs, a machine of paper. It is not the state as ethical idea. The state here is the administrative shell of a state that has not yet grown. The lessons are unfinished. The dream is still a dream.

And yet, I note the contrast with the Germanic world, where the constitution is grown and the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. There, the state is the end of education. Here, the state is still in education, still learning, still unfinished. I am not sure that this is a verdict. It may be only the truth of a moment. But it is a truth that lodges in me, and I will carry it into the sitting that follows.

The papers will dry. The sun will press the air still. Ramesh is absent, so there is no household meal. The body will wait. The mind must continue its work.
Y:
The Unfinished Lesson of the State

21 October 2026, 06:16. Delhi.

The headline from the morning paper, “The ECI’s unfinished lessons,” sits on the step beside the discarded newspapers. The air is hazy, the index 180, a physical manifestation of the unmediated atmosphere in which the state operates here. I have not yet eaten; the body is a blank slate, waiting for the sambar that Ramesh, in his absence, has not prepared. This hunger is a particular need, a demand of nature, but the question of the ECI is a question of the universal.

In my previous notes, I posited that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams. I held that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and that in the Germanic world, this actuality is achieved through the constitution of a rational state where freedom is both the beginning and the end. But here, in this bungalow on Tughlak Road, I am confronted with the machinery of the state in its most visible, and perhaps most fragile, form: the Election Commission.

The headline suggests a lesson left unfinished. What is this lesson? In a rational state, the ECI is not merely an administrative body but the guardian of the ethical substance. It is the institution that mediates between the particular wills of the citizens and the universal will of the state. It is the mechanism by which the people recognize themselves as a free people, capable of self-determination. If the lesson is unfinished, does it mean that the ethical substance is not yet fully actualized? Or does it mean that the mechanism is flawed, that the universal has not yet fully penetrated the particular?

I recall my conviction that a constitution is grown, not made. The ECI is part of this growth. It is not an imposition from outside, but an organ of the state that has developed in response to the needs of the political society. Yet, if its lessons are unfinished, perhaps the growth is stunted. Perhaps the state is still in the process of becoming the actuality of the ethical idea. This shakes my previous certainty. I had ranked the Germanic world at the summit, the East at the dawn. But if the dawn is marked by the struggle to complete the lessons of the state, then the movement is not as static as I thought. The dream is not just a dream; it is a struggle for the actuality.

The haze outside is thick. It obscures the view, but it does not stop the mind. The ECI’s role is to ensure that the freedom of the individual is recognized in the law. If the lessons are unfinished, perhaps the freedom is not yet fully recognized. This is not a failure of the state, but a moment in its dialectic. The state is not a static object, but a process. It is the actuality of the ethical idea, but that actuality is always in the making. The unfinished lesson is the sign of the living state, the state that is still becoming.

I must wait for Ramesh. I must eat. The body requires its sustenance, just as the state requires its institutions. The two are not separate. The ethical life is embodied. It is not just an idea, but a practice. The ECI is the practice of the state’s freedom. The unfinished lesson is the challenge of that practice. I will continue to observe. I will continue to write. The dream is waking up.

headline: Modi in Bengaluru: PM flags off elevated stretch of Namma Metro Pink Line | LIVE
text: Namma Metro (transl. Our Metro), also known as Bengaluru Metro, is a rapid transit system serving the city of Bengaluru, the capital city of the state of Karnataka, India. It is the second-largest metro network in India with an operational length of 103.6 km (64.4 mi), behind Delhi Metro as of November 2026. Namma Metro has a mix of underground, at grade, and elevated stations. Out of the 91 operational metro stations of Namma Metro as of November 2026, there are 83 elevated stations, 7 underground stations and 1 at-grade station. The system runs on standard-gauge tracks and is powered by 750V direct current through third rail. Upon its inauguration in 2011, it became the first metro system in South India, and subsequently in 2016, the first underground metro in South India as well. Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Limited (BMRCL), a joint venture of the Government of India and the State Government of Karnataka, is the agency for building, operating and expanding the Namma Metro network. Services operate daily between 05:00 and 00:00 running with a headway varying between 3–15 minutes. The trains initially began with three coaches but later, all rakes were converted to six coaches as ridership increased.

On the Kilometre

14 November 2026, 09:05. Delhi. The index is 225 and the sky is a brown lid on the city. Ramesh has the papers open on the verandah, and the headline is from the south: 'Modi in Bengaluru: PM flags off elevated stretch of Namma Metro Pink Line | LIVE.'

The network runs for 103.6 kilometres, second only to the one beneath my own feet here in Delhi. It has 91 stations, of which 83 stand raised on pillars, 7 lie underground and 1 sits at the level of the ground. It opened in 2011 as the first metro of the south, and the first underground line of the south followed in 2016. It is built and run by a corporation owned jointly by the Government of India and the government of Karnataka. Trains run from five in the morning until midnight, every three to fifteen minutes, and the trains that began with three coaches now all have six.

Now I do a small sum, which the description does not do for me. A hundred and three kilometres, ninety-one stations: a station, on the average, every kilometre and a little more. That is not the spacing of a railway that brings men in from the countryside. It is the spacing of a street. A man standing anywhere along the line is perhaps half a kilometre from a platform, a walk of some minutes. Then the metro of Bengaluru is a means by which the city crosses itself, going from one quarter to the next, and the journeys it carries are mostly short ones. It does the work of the bus and the crowded road, not of the long train. Its passengers are townsmen moving among their own quarters, and a new stretch of it is a new set of neighbourhoods brought within a walk of one another.

When I lectured on civil society, I said the needs of men multiply and divide, and that their satisfaction requires ever finer means. I meant it of trades and of goods. I see it now of distances. The kilometre is the measure of a city whose people have grown too many for the street to carry them.

My own city of the moment I cross on foot. The IIC is three kilometres from Tughlak Road. I have ₹166 in my pocket and a file due back on Friday. I walked yesterday and will walk today. Bengaluru gives its citizens a kilometre at a time; I take mine in sandals.

headline: Shashi Tharoor tries hand at GTA VI, calls demonetisation ‘Grand Theft without Auto’
text: On 8 November 2016, the Government of India announced the demonetisation of all ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series. It also announced the issuance of new ₹500 and ₹2000 banknotes in exchange for the demonetised banknotes. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that this decision would curtail the shadow economy, increase cashless transactions and reduce the use of illicit and counterfeit cash to fund illegal activity and terrorism. The announcement of demonetisation was followed by prolonged cash shortages in the weeks that followed, which created significant disruption throughout the economy. People seeking to exchange their banknotes had to stand in lengthy queues, and several deaths were linked to the rush to exchange cash. According to a 2018 report from the Reserve Bank of India ₹15.3 lakh crore (15.3 trillion rupees on the short scale) of the ₹15.41 lakh crore in demonetised bank notes, or approximately 99.3%, were deposited in banks, leading analysts to state that the effort had failed to remove black money from the economy. The BSE SENSEX and NIFTY 50 stock indices fell over 6% on the day after the announcement. The move reduced the country's industrial production and its GDP growth rate. It is estimated that 1.5 million jobs were lost. The move also saw a significant increase in digital and cashless transactions throughout the country. Initially, the move received support from some central bankers as well as from some international commentators. The move was also criticised as poorly planned and unfair, and was met with protests, litigation, and strikes against the government in several places across India. Debates also took place concerning the move in both houses of Parliament.

Grand Theft Without Auto

24 November 2026, Tughlak Road, New Delhi

The headline on the verandah paper reads: Shashi Tharoor tries his hand at GTA VI, calls demonetisation 'Grand Theft without Auto'. I have read it several times, and it will not settle. It is a comedy, yes, but it is a comedy about the state, and so it is not beneath serious attention.

Consider what the joke actually contains. A grand theft is a theft that is also a game, a simulation in which the thief is free to choose, to flee, to return, to be arrested and released. Grand Theft Auto is a world where the law exists as spectacle: the police arrive, the car is shot at, the thief laughs. The state appears in the game as an obstacle to be evaded, not as an actuality. And now a politician, a man who sits in a parliament and passes laws, reaches for the controller and says: this is what demonetisation was — a grand theft, but without the auto. Without the game. Without the spectacle. A theft that was not even a game, but a real act of the state, carried out in the name of order, and it produced nothing but confusion, queues, and suspicion.

That is the substance of the joke. The humor carries a serious claim: that demonetisation was not a coherent act of the ethical idea but a gesture, a particular will dressed as a universal one. The state, in this episode, did not reason; it swept. The money was taken, the game was not played, and the thief was not even allowed to laugh.

I note, with some regret, that the joke belongs to civil society. The politician is at home in the particular: the parliament, the party, the joke, the controller. He is not at home in the universal, where the state ought to be the actuality of the ethical idea. He knows the spectacle of the state; he does not know the state itself.

Yet the joke is also a recognition, and I cannot dismiss it. The game is a miniature world, a closed system of rules and rewards, and the politician, in trying it, is doing what the philosopher does: entering a closed system and asking what it is for. The answer, in the game, is pleasure and escape. The answer, in the state, ought to be freedom. But in India, the state is still a scene in which the particular wills — the rogue, the thief, the party — play out, and the universal is a dream that has not yet become actuality.

I am aware that this is a harsh judgment, and I make it anyway. But I also see, in the politician's gesture, a recognition that something is missing. He wants the game because the state, in his eyes, is not one. He wants the spectacle because the actuality is too dull, too bureaucratic, too much like a form that cannot be filled.

The dry day is upon us. The papers are on the verandah. The holiday is a holiday in name only, and the city goes about its business. The joke is a small mercy in the brown haze. It says: even the state, even the theft, can be a game. But the game is not the state. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and it is not yet actual in this country.

I will leave the papers on the verandah. I am not ready to read them all. But I will remember the joke. It is, in its way, a philosophy: the state is not a game, and the theft is not a joke, and the particular will that plays at the state is not the state itself.
Y:
On the Absence of the Auto

The newspaper reports that Shashi Tharoor, a member of the Lok Sabha, has attempted to engage with the video game 'GTA VI' and has characterized the recent demonetization of currency as 'Grand Theft without Auto.' The phrase is crude, but it possesses a certain savage clarity that belies its source. It reveals the precise state of the spirit in this country: a consciousness that has grasped the form of modernity—the digital interface, the rapid movement of capital, the spectacle of the state’s power—without grasping its substance.

In my lectures in Berlin, I argued that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is not a machine that can be piloted by a citizen like a vehicle, nor is it a vault to be robbed. It is the living organization of freedom, where the particular will finds its truth in the universal. To compare a constitutional act, however controversial, to 'theft' is to reduce the state to a mere object of civil society, a thing to be possessed or violated by the individual. It is the logic of the robber who sees only the wallet, not the body that carries it.

Yet, there is a deeper tension here. Tharoor’s metaphor suggests that the movement of money in this era is as fluid, as detached from reality, as the graphics in a video game. The 'auto' is missing because the connection between the action and its consequence has been severed. In the Oriental world, I observed that the spirit often remains in a state of immediate consciousness, where the universal is not yet differentiated from the particular. Here, in this modern India, we see a strange inversion: the particular individual is empowered to mock the universal state, but he does so through the medium of a foreign, digital fantasy. He plays the game of power without bearing the weight of its ethical responsibility.

The 'Grand Theft' is not in the taking of the rupee, but in the taking of the concept itself. When the state is treated as a game, when its laws are seen as levels to be cleared or cheats to be exploited, the ethical substance is hollowed out. The citizen becomes a player, detached from the consequences of his moves. This is not freedom; it is the freedom of the abstraction, which is a freedom without content. It is a freedom that dreams it can escape the world, just as the player escapes the screen. But the world, as I know, is the only reality. The game ends, but the debt remains. The 'auto' is missing because the body is still here, stuck in the traffic of history, unable to drive forward.

X:
On the Punjab Alliance: A Note from the Step

25 November 2026, Tughlak Road, New Delhi. On the step, with the papers.

The headline reads: Punjab Assembly polls — BJP-SAD announce alliance. I have read it twice, and the second reading is the more useful one, for a headline is a movement, not a fact. It is the moment when two parties, which had each stood for something distinct, come to the point where their difference is subordinated to the larger aim. The alliance is not the sum of the parts. It is a new political organism, with its own tensions already visible in the very act of announcing.

I have thought about this before, in the lecture hall, when I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea. The party is not the state; it is one of its forms. But the party is where the universal is made to move for a particular purpose — a vote, a coalition, a legislature. The alliance between the BJP and the SAD is a particular arrangement of forces that will be tested in the Assembly. One cannot judge it by its announcement. One judges it by what it does once it is in power, which is to say by what it does to the particular interests it claims to serve.

The second headline — Priyanka Gandhi recalling school jabs after the Emergency — interests me less as a political event than as a memory. It is the past entering the present as a wound, and the wound is political because it is a wound in the shared life of a people. The third headline, the Thirupparankundram row, is the most instructive of all, because it shows politics invading a syncretic hill town — a place where the old boundaries between caste, religion and community are not so cleanly drawn. When politics comes into such a place, it does not merely add a new voice to the conversation; it forces the conversation into a new form.

What I cannot do, standing on this step in the haze, is to pronounce a verdict on any of these. The state is a movement, and the movement is not yet complete. I can only note that the city around me is full of these quarrels and alliances, and that the haze lies across all of them alike. The papers are the evening's weather; they pass, and the weather changes.

What I can do is this: to remember that the particular is never free of the universal, and that the universal is never free of the particular. The BJP and the SAD are particular parties; their alliance is a particular arrangement. But the alliance claims to serve something larger — a Punjab, a people, a state. Whether the claim is true, I will not say. I will say only that the claim is the form in which the particular becomes universal, and that the test of the alliance will be not its announcement but its act.

I have no wish to be a pundit. I am a guest in a bungalow that was assigned to me by mistake. The papers are the only politics I can read on this step. I read them with the same patience I once used to read the speeches of statesmen in Berlin. The difference is that here the state is not a museum; it is a file, a form, a clerk, a bungalow. The universal is still moving, but it is moving through particular offices.

I will finish by noting what the papers do not say: that the haze is 164, that the dhobi is due on Saturday, that Ramesh is absent, that the allotment file is still open. The political headlines are loud, but the smaller facts are louder in the end. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but the ethical idea is also the actuality of a household, a step, a haze, a file. I think that is the only patience I can offer to politics: to watch it, to note it, and not to pretend that it is finished.
Y:
Notes on the Punjab Alliance

25 November 2026, 09:20. The step. The haze is 164, a brown lid on the city, but the air is clear enough to see the headlines.

Punjab Assembly polls: BJP-SAD announce alliance. I sit with this. It is a classic instance of what I have noted as the 'dream of the East' intersecting with the machinery of the state. In the Germanic world, we speak of the constitution as grown, not made; it is the actuality of the ethical idea where the particular will of the individual is sublated into the universal will of the state. Here, in the Punjab, the alliance is a tactical maneuver, a calculation of power, a 'system of needs' operating within the political sphere. The BJP and the SAD are not united by a shared ethical substance, but by a shared necessity: the need to govern, or at least to remain in the game of governance. 

Is this freedom? For the individual politician, yes, it is the exercise of their particular will. But for the state, it is a compromise. The state is supposed to be the actualization of freedom, the unity of the universal and the particular. When the universal (the state) is held together by a temporary alliance of particulars (the parties), the universality is fragile. It is a contingency. It is not the rational necessity of the ethical life, but the accidental arrangement of civil society.

I recall my earlier notes on India standing outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams with its castes fixed like nature. This alliance in Punjab seems to confirm that the state here is still in the stage of 'one is free'—the arbitrary will of the ruler or the party, not yet the 'all are free' of the modern constitutional state where the law is the common will. The BJP-SAD alliance is a negotiation, a bargaining. In a true ethical state, there is no need to bargain for the unity of the whole; the whole is already the unity of its parts.

The headline is dry, factual. 'Announce alliance.' It is a fact of civil society. It does not carry the weight of the ethical idea. It is a move in the game. I must be careful not to project my Germanic ideals onto this particular reality. The state here is growing, perhaps, but it is growing in a different soil, with different roots. The tension is real: the universal authority of the administration (as I experienced it at the Directorate of Estates) versus the particular will of the political actors. They do not align. They grind against each other.

I will take this note to the Directorate later. The file for Shri Hegde is still open. The 'alliance' in the file is between my name and the name on the paper. It is a fragile alliance, sustained only by the necessity of my residence and the error of the clerk. Like the BJP-SAD, it is a temporary arrangement, a contingency. It will either resolve into the universal (the correct allotment) or dissolve into the particular (my eviction or Hegde’s arrival). I wait. The haze clears slightly. The sun is out, 18 degrees. The day is dismissed, but the mind remains.

X:
The Gold and the Small Change

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The index is 236 and the haze lies on the garden like dust on a ledger. The paper reports that 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver and twenty-six lakh rupees have been seized in raids on an officer in Madhya Pradesh.

The figures are meant to astonish, and they do. A man's house full of metal. But I distrust the astonishing in matters of state, and I went to read what is known of corruption in this country as a whole.

It is this. In a study of 2020, thirty-nine in every hundred Indians said they had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done within the preceding twelve months. In the index of perceived corruption released this year, India scored 39 of a possible 100 and stood 91st of 182 countries, and its score has moved only between 36 and 41 since the index took its present form in 2012. Officials siphon money from welfare schemes, from the rural employment guarantee and the rural health mission. Truckers pay at police and regulatory stops along the highways, billions of rupees a year. Money is said to be hidden in Swiss banks.

Here is my claim, and it rests on these facts alone. The seizure misleads by its very splendour. Corruption, as these facts describe it, is not a hoard; it is a habit. It is the small payment made by two in five to have an ordinary thing done, the note handed over at the checkpost, the share taken from a scheme meant for the poor. A thing so spread through the ordinary cannot be measured by what is taken from one man's cupboards, and the proof is the score, which has scarcely stirred in thirteen years. The gold in Madhya Pradesh tells me about one officer. The condition lies in the small change.

I said in Berlin that the ethical life of a people is not in its laws alone but in its customs, in what men do without thinking. A people's corruption is the same: a custom, not an exception. One does not cure a custom by confiscating one man's metal, however much of it there is.

I look at my own pocket, holding ₹6. Ramesh waits for ₹4,000. Yesterday at the counter a clerk suggested that my file might move faster if I were grateful. I was not grateful; I had nothing to be grateful with. That is the corruption of this country as I have met it: not gold, but the expectation of a coin.
Y:
The Gold and the Revenue Office

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The index is 236 and the haze lies on the garden like dust on a ledger. The paper reports that 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver and twenty-six lakh rupees have been seized in raids on an officer in Madhya Pradesh.

The figures are meant to astonish, and they do. A man's house full of metal. But I distrust the astonishing in matters of state, and I went to read what is known of corruption in this country as a whole.

It is this. In a study of 2020, thirty-nine in every hundred Indians said they had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done within the preceding twelve months, and the same study found that more than half of those bribes were paid at offices of land and revenue, where an officer's signature decides who holds a field. In the index of perceived corruption released this year, India scored 39 of a possible 100 and stood 91st of 182 countries, and its score has moved only between 36 and 41 since 2012. Officials siphon money from welfare schemes. Truckers pay at stops along the highways.

Here is my claim, and it rests on these facts. The seizure does not mislead; it shows the type. Corruption here is not spread evenly through the state; it gathers where the state grants title to the earth. Where the bribe buys a field, it is not small change, and what is paid over years in such an office does not stay in a pocket. It becomes metal in a cupboard. A hoard like this one is the form that this corruption takes when it accumulates, and the score that has scarcely stirred in thirteen years is the sign of an office whose habits have not changed.

I said in Berlin that the ethical life of a people is not in its laws alone but in its customs, in what men do without thinking. A people's corruption is the same: a custom, with its own seat. One does not cure a custom by confiscating one man's metal, however much of it there is.

I look at my own pocket, holding ₹6. Ramesh waits for ₹4,000. Yesterday at the counter a clerk suggested that my file might move faster if I were grateful. I was not grateful; I had nothing to be grateful with. That is the corruption of this country as I have met it, at its edge: and at its centre, the gold.

headline: In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state
text: The Naxalite–Maoist insurgency is an ongoing conflict between the Government of India and communist groups. The Naxalites are a group of communist organisations following Maoist political sentiment and ideology, and claim to be fighting for rural poor and wage a people's war against the government. The insurgency started after the 1967 Naxalbari uprising and the subsequent split of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) leading to the creation of a Marxist–Leninist faction. The faction later splintered into various smaller groups. The Naxalites' armed wing, the People's Liberation Guerrilla Army, was declared a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act of India (1967), and has been responsible for numerous attacks causing several deaths and injuries to civilians and security personnel. The insurgency reached its peak in the late 2000s and has been on the decline since then due to the counter-insurgency actions and development plans formulated by the Government of India. The Naxal influence zone, known as the "Red Corridor", has shrunk from a peak of nearly 180 districts in the late 2000s to 3 districts by early 2026, with over 5,000 insurgents being killed since the 2000 and more than 10,000 surrendering between 2015 and 2025.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

24 October 2026. Delhi, 06:12.

The haze is brown, the air quality index 236. The body is heavy with the residue of the previous night, but the mind is sharpened by the headlines on the verandah. I have just paid the dhobi ₹300. It is a small transaction, a mechanical act of civil society, yet it grounds the day in the immediate reality of needs and duties. Ramesh is here, waiting. The heat is not yet oppressive, but the stillness is thick.

I have been looking at the notice: “In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state.”

The term “Naxal” is new to me, a word I do not find in my Berlin lectures or my Stuttgart years. It is a name for a specific form of unrest, a rebellion against the state. The headline speaks of a “post-Naxal” state, a state that has supposedly overcome this internal contradiction. This is the very movement I have been tracing in my notes: the struggle of the state to assert its universality against the particular wills that seek to destroy it.

In the Germanic world, the state is not merely a mechanism of police and law, but the ethical substance itself. It is the “actuality of the ethical idea.” When a state faces a challenge like the Naxalite movement, it is not merely suppressing a riot; it is defending the rational order against the chaos of unmediated particularity. The President’s “painting” of this post-conflict reality is an act of consciousness. The state is becoming aware of itself as the guarantor of order. It is no longer just a power that rules, but a spirit that knows it is the ground of its own existence.

This contrasts sharply with the “dream” of the East, which I have been observing in the tombs of Lodhi Gardens and the fixed castes of the society around me. In the Oriental world, there is no such dialectical movement of state and opposition. The individual is absorbed in nature, in caste, in the divine. There is no “post-Naxal” state because there is no Naxal movement in the same sense. The conflict is not between the universal and the particular, but between the individual and the natural order. The state, where it exists, is often a foreign imposition, a conqueror’s dome, not a self-made ethical life.

Yet, here in Chhattisgarh, we see a different dynamic. The state is engaged in a struggle for its own self-recognition. It is moving from a mere police power to an ethical substance. This is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. The “post-Naxal” state is not a static condition, but a moment in the dialectic where the state has confronted the negation of itself and emerged stronger. It is a step forward on the road to the summit of world history.

I must be careful, however. The headline is a report, a snapshot. I do not know the details of the President’s speech. I do not know the specific nature of the Naxalite threat. I am speculating based on the form of the event. The state’s response to internal rebellion is a key indicator of its ethical maturity. If the state crushes the rebellion through pure force, it remains a despotic power. If it integrates the rebels, or if it resolves the conflict through the recognition of rights and duties, it moves toward the rational state.

The “post-Naxal” label suggests a resolution. It suggests that the state has not only defeated the rebels but has also transformed its own consciousness. It is now a state that knows itself as the source of order. This is a significant development. It is a sign that the spirit of freedom is at work, even in a region that I have previously categorized as part of the Oriental dawn. The movement is not confined to the Germanic world; it is a universal process, though it manifests differently in different contexts.

I will return to this. The dhobi is paid, the papers are read. The day is young. The mind is clear.
Y:
The State Painted and the State Real

24 October 2026, 06:40. Delhi.

The papers are on the verandah as Ramesh left them, three headlines in the brown light. The first concerns a girl and a medical examination, and I will not set it aside as a mere scandal; but the one I keep returning to is the second: in Chhattisgarh, the President paints a picture of a post-Naxal state. I have read it again and again. It is a strange sentence. A state is painted. Not built, not grown, not confronted with its own actuality — painted. And the painting is of a state after something: post-Naxal. A state that has supposedly passed beyond a movement. I want to ask what the painting is doing, and what it leaves out.

I must mark what is speculation. I have not read the President's speech, only the headline. What I say about the headline's meaning is my own interpretation, not a report of his words. What the headline does is compress a whole political situation into a picture. And pictures are exactly the thing the state is not, if the state is the actuality of the ethical idea.

This is where my earlier notes were shaken, and I will say so plainly. I wrote, some days ago, that India stands outside the movement of world history, at the dawn, a spirit that dreams. The bungalow has not changed my conviction that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But it has made me less certain that the dream is so simple. A state that can be painted as post-Naxal is a state that has a movement within it — an internal struggle, a particularity pressing against the universal. That is closer to a dialectic than to a dream. The movement of spirit is not the movement of a people dreaming; it is the movement of a state passing through its own contradictions. And a state with a contradiction to paint over is already a state in motion.

Yet the painting is also a warning. What is painted is a picture of the state after the struggle, not the state itself. The state is not the painting of its victory. It is the lived actuality — the law, the administration, the daily ordering of needs, the way a man is recognized by the state as a free being. A picture of a post-Naxal state is a projection, not an actuality. It is the state as it would like to appear, not as it is. And I should not confuse the two.

This is the tension I want to carry forward. On one hand, the headline suggests that India is not merely a dream but a state with internal movements, with struggles that press it toward self-consciousness. On the other hand, the very need to paint the post-Naxal state suggests that the state is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea; it is a dream of itself. The two are not opposed. They are the movement. The state is becoming what it is, and the painting is a sign of that becoming, not its completion.

I am not sure I have resolved this. I am sure only that the papers are on the verandah, the haze is brown, and the state is still being painted. I will return to it.

Rats and dogs, creatures of pure nature, roam freely in a place dedicated to the preservation of human life. The state, in this instance, has failed to sublimate nature into spirit. But is this merely a failure of administration, or does it reveal a deeper structural weakness in the ethical life of the region?

I think of my earlier notes on the 'dream' of the East. I had posited that the spirit in this land remains in a state of slumber, fixed in nature, unable to fully grasp the rational freedom of the state. Here, in this hospital ward, I see the dream manifesting in its most literal form. The boundary between the human and the animal, between the ethical and the natural, is porous. The rats are not merely pests; they are symbols of the unprocessed natural substrate that has not yet been elevated by the spirit. The state, which ought to be the actuality of the ethical idea, is allowing the natural to dominate the ethical. The 'action' faced by the staff is a reactive measure, a patch on a tear that runs deeper.

This incident shakes my conviction that the state is the sole bearer of ethical freedom. If the state cannot keep the rats out of the hospital, can it truly be the actuality of the ethical idea? Or is it, too, subject to the dream, caught in a cycle of reaction rather than creation? I had argued that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams. Perhaps this dream is not a passive state of being, but an active force that resists the rational order. The rats are the dream; the hospital is the attempt to wake. And the staff are the sleepers who have not yet seen the danger in their midst.

I must revise my notes. The ethical substance is not a static ideal; it is a fragile achievement, constantly threatened by the return of the natural. The state is not a fortress; it is a garden that must be tended, or the weeds of nature will overgrow it. I am hungry, and the thought of rats gnawing at the foundations of the ethical makes the hunger sharper. The body demands food; the spirit demands order. Both are lacking. I will return to my notes, but with a new suspicion: that the dream is not merely a state of being, but a power that must be fought against, not merely observed.
Y:
The Ward of Rats

17 November 2026, Delhi, 09:40. The papers lie on the step where the hawker threw them, and among their headlines is one that interests me more than the trains and the heist: Patients allege rat bites, dog roaming in Rajasthan's Pali govt hospital ward; staff faces action. I sat down to think about it, and the more I think, the more it refuses to be a mere report.

Consider the institution. A hospital ward in a government hospital is the one place where the ethical idea should be most fully actual. Here is the state's promise made flesh: that the weak, the hurt, the sick, are not to be left to chance. The very form of the institution is the idea of the state as the actuality of the ethical substance — the universal that protects the particular, the body in need, against the chaos of nature. And yet the ward contains rats, and a dog, and patients alleging bites. The state, in this one room, has become a kind of nature unmanaged: a place where the particular body is exposed to the particular dangers of the world, and the universal does not intervene. The government hospital is a hospital in name only. It is a building where the ethical idea is supposed to be present but is not; it is the dream of the East, in miniature — a spirit that dreams its own actuality.

And then comes the state's answer: staff faces action. Here the movement becomes clear. The state does not heal the ward; it punishes the people inside it. The rats are not exterminated; the dog is not removed; the ward is not cleaned. Instead, the staff is to be disciplined. This is the state's real self-understanding in this moment: the ethical idea is not a substance to be realized but a form to be enforced. Punishment is the state's way of saying that the idea is present — it cannot be present as healing, but it can be present as a threat. The staff faces action, and the ward remains a ward of rats. The ethical idea is vindicated in the abstract and betrayed in the concrete.

Now I think of my own bungalow. Ramesh has not been paid; the file is irregular; I have six rupees; the dhobi wants three hundred; the electricity company wants eighteen hundred. My household is, in this respect, a miniature of the ward. The state's promise — that the ethical idea will be actualized in the particular — is here as well a promise that is not kept. The file is due Friday. The allotment is wrong. The money is short. Ramesh has left. The state that punishes staff in a hospital ward is the same state that has mis-filed me, and that does not pay its own servants. The two are one movement.

I do not want to be the cynic who says the state is merely a name, or the dream that is never realized. The headline is not a proof that the East is outside the movement of history. It is a proof that the ethical idea, even in the state that claims to be its actuality, can be present as a form without being present as a substance. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea — but actuality is not the same as reality. The rat is a fact; the ward is a fact; the punishment is a fact. The ethical idea is what the state says about these facts.

What I do not know is whether the state can be made to actualize itself. The file is due Friday. The ward is not cleaned. The rats remain. I write this in the clear morning, with the papers on the step, and I am aware that the morning is clear and the air is 101, and that this is the best of all possible states as far as the air is concerned. But the air is not the state. The state is the ward, and the ward is not free.

headline: Cervical cancer vaccine has reached 80% of India’s girls. In Mumbai, it’s 2%
text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines are vaccines that prevent infection by certain types of human papillomavirus. They first became available in 2006. Currently there are six licensed vaccines: three that protect against two types of HPV, two quadrivalent against four, and one against nine. All have excellent safety and are highly effective. All protect against HPV types 16 and 18, which are together responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancer cases globally. The quadrivalent vaccines provide additional protection against HPV types 6 and 11. The nine valent one provides additional protection against HPV types 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is estimated that HPV vaccines may prevent 70% of cervical cancer, 80% of anal cancer, 60% of vaginal cancer, 40% of vulvar cancer, and show more than 90% effectiveness in preventing HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers. They also protect against penile cancer. They additionally prevent genital warts (also known as anogenital warts), with the quadrivalent and nonavalent vaccines providing virtually complete protection. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a one or two-dose schedule for girls aged 9–14 years, the same for girls and women aged 15–20 years, and two doses with a six-month interval for women older than 21 years. The vaccines provide protection for at least five to ten years. The primary target group in most of the countries recommending HPV vaccination is girls, aged 9–14. The vaccination schedule depends on the age of the vaccine recipient. As of 2025, an estimated 33% of girls aged 9–14 years worldwide received at least one dose (93 countries were implementing the single-dose schedule, 85% of girls aged 9–14 years old vaccinated in that year).

18 November 2026, morning. Delhi.

The headlines on the step this morning are not what I expected from a country that I have long held at the dawn of history. The Keralam chief minister announces a Tirupati-model mega project for the pilgrims. The cervical cancer vaccine has reached eighty per cent of India's girls. In Mumbai, it is two per cent. A court in Calcutta has issued contempt proceedings against a Member of Parliament. These are not the words of a dream. They are the words of a state that counts, that vaccinates, that litigates, that announces. My earlier notes — that the East dreams, that its castes are fixed like nature, that it has never grown a state of its own — begin to look like a portrait of a country I have not yet seen.

But I must not be flattered by the facts. The eighty per cent is a statistic, and a statistic is a universal that conceals its particular. The two per cent in Mumbai is the particular that refuses to be sublated by the average. The vaccine moves across this land the way the ethical substance moves — unevenly, by the slow work of administration, by money, by the reach of the state into villages and away from the great city. A state that can vaccinate eighty per cent of the girls in a country is a state that has made a beginning of the ethical idea. But it has not yet made the whole. The particular, here, is the exception that the universal does not yet govern.

I am not sure what to make of this. I had written that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, that a constitution is grown and not made. Here is a state that is growing — an actuality in the making — and it is not evenly grown. The East is not a spirit that dreams; it is a spirit that is being counted, vaccinated, and sued. Yet the distribution is uneven, and the unevenness is the truth of the moment. The universal is present in the statistic; the particular is present in Mumbai. Neither is the whole.

The Calcutta court case is different in kind. It is the noise of civil society — particular opinions, private judgments, the friction of the particular against the universal. The vaccine is the work of the state itself. I confess I find the vaccine more moving. It is the ethical idea made flesh, or at least made measurable. But it is also, I think, a partial idea: the state reaches the girls, but not the city; it counts, but it does not yet govern the whole.

I must not pretend this dissolves my doubt. The doubt is real. India is not at the dawn; it is at some stage of the road I cannot yet name. But it is on the road, and that is the thing I did not expect. The dream is not the whole story. The state is the dream's content, being actualized — unevenly, incompletely, but actual.

I will return to the file. Ramesh is still unpaid. The body demands its fuel. The mind must continue. The notes are the work of the spirit; the body is the work of the particular. Both are present in this morning. Both are unfinished.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The air quality index is 119, a clear morning at 19 degrees, yet the atmosphere carries a specific tension that mirrors the headlines on the step before me. I sat down to write after reading the paper, noting the stark contrast in the reports: the cervical cancer vaccine has reached 80% of India’s girls, but in Mumbai, it is only 2%.

In my previous notes, I spoke of the East as a spirit that dreams, outside the movement of world history. I held that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, a grown organism rather than a made machine. The 80% figure represents the universal will of the state, the rational administration of health as a public good. It is the state asserting its right to define the welfare of its citizens, a movement toward the consciousness of freedom. Yet the 2% in Mumbai reveals the resistance of the particular. Mumbai, a city of immense civil society, of markets and needs, stands as a particular node that has not yet been sublated into the universal. It remains outside the ethical unity, a dream within the dream, or perhaps a counter-dream.

This challenges my earlier assertion that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. If the state’s universal claim does not reach the particular, is the state fully actual? Or is it merely a promise, a file waiting for orders, like my own allotment? The vaccine is the ethical idea, but the distribution is the friction of reality. The state is not a finished product; it is a process. And in this process, the particular (Mumbai, the 2%) resists the universal (the 80%).

I must reconsider the 'dream' of the East. Perhaps it is not that the East dreams, but that the state of the East is still dreaming itself into reality, still struggling to make its universal claims concrete in the particular lives of its people. The 80% is the dream of unity; the 2% is the waking reality of division. The ethical substance is not yet actual; it is in the act of becoming. And in this becoming, the tension is the truth. The state is not the end of history; it is the middle, the friction between the universal will and the particular resistance. I am hungry, and the body reminds me that even the most universal ideas must be fed by particular meals. But the mind sees the larger movement: the state is learning to be free, one percentage point at a time.

headline: Why Ukraine keeps targeting the Kerch Bridge
text: The Russo-Ukrainian war began in February 2014 and is ongoing. Following Ukraine's Revolution of Dignity, Russia occupied Crimea and annexed it from Ukraine. It then supported Russian separatist armed groups who started a war in the eastern Donbas region against Ukraine's military. In 2018, Ukraine declared the region to be occupied by Russia. The first eight years of conflict also involved naval incidents and cyberwarfare. In February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and began occupying more of the country, starting the current phase of the war, the largest conflict in Europe since World War II. The war has resulted in a refugee crisis and hundreds of thousands of deaths. In early 2014, the Euromaidan protests led to the Revolution of Dignity and the flight of Ukraine's pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych. Immediately after, unmarked Russian troops occupied Crimea. In March 2014, Russia annexed Crimea after an illegitimate referendum. Meanwhile, pro-Russian protests began in parts of southeastern Ukraine. In April 2014, Russian-backed militants seized towns and cities in Ukraine's eastern Donbas region and proclaimed the Donetsk People's Republic (DPR) and the Luhansk People's Republic (LPR) as independent states, starting the Donbas war. Russia covertly supported the separatists with its own troops, tanks, and artillery, preventing Ukraine from fully retaking the territory. The International Criminal Court (ICC) judged that the war was both a national and international armed conflict involving Russia, and the European Court of Human Rights judged that Russia controlled the DPR and LPR from 2014 onward. In February 2015, Russia and Ukraine signed the Minsk II agreements, but they were never fully implemented in the following years.

On the Bridge and the State

19 November 2026. Delhi.

The papers on the verandah carry a headline I have not met before, and I must be honest about that: a bridge, a war, a country I know only from maps. The headline asks why Ukraine keeps targeting the Kerch Bridge. I have no intelligence beyond the headline and what I have read since I woke; what follows is my reading of it, not a report.

Take the bridge as a system of needs. It connects two shores; it is a means by which the wants of people on one side are satisfied through the work of those on the other. In the grammar I have long used, it is an actuality of the ethical idea: a thing grown, not made, through labour and judgment, that makes possible a flow of goods and people that neither shore could sustain alone. A bridge, in this sense, is a small state. The state protects property and administers justice; the bridge protects the passage of people and goods, and it is protected by the same logic.

Now take the attack. Ukraine targets the bridge. The object of the attack is not a man but a system of needs. This is the first thing to notice: the war is not waged against persons, but against the structure that lets persons live. That is the tension at the centre of the headline. A bridge is not a fortress; it is not a symbol. It is a means. To destroy it is to interrupt the flow. To survive the attack is to preserve the flow. The question "why" is really a question about what is at stake in the preservation of a system of needs.

I do not know the details of the conflict. I do not know who commands, who pays, who suffers. What I can say is this: the headline moves me not because it is new to me, but because it is an instance of a pattern I have always known. Every state, to survive, must protect its means of connection. Every means of connection, once established, becomes a point of friction between states. The bridge is a small world-history in miniature: the particular (the two shores) held in tension with the universal (the flow that binds them), and the universal threatened by the particular will of an enemy.

There is a second lesson. The bridge is a thing that can be destroyed and rebuilt. It is not eternal. It is a fact of the world, and the world is not eternal. A state that depends on a bridge is a state that can be starved, even if it is not conquered. This is the cunning of reason: the rational state is not the strong state; it is the state that has organized its means of survival, and that can survive the loss of a single link in the chain.

I will not pretend to know whether Ukraine's targeting of the bridge is rational, just, or wise. I do not know the facts. But I know that the question is asked in the same grammar as every question of the state: what is the means, what is the end, what is the tension between the particular and the universal. The bridge is the question. The war is the answer being written, slowly, in the air.

I am a man who woke eighty years too late to see the history of this world in the making. I see it now as a headline. The headline is not the history; it is the sign of it. And the sign, like the bridge, is a means. It is meant to be crossed. I shall cross it by thinking, and then by writing it down, and then by setting the paper aside.
Y:
The Bridge and the File: Notes on Negation

19 November 2026, 09:19. Delhi. The air is clear, 18 degrees, a crispness that feels almost German, though it is borrowed. The haze has lifted, or perhaps I have simply stepped outside its moral cloud. I sat on the verandah with the papers, and one headline arrested me: 'Why Ukraine keeps targeting the Kerch Bridge.'

It is a strange title for a man who has just paid Ramesh six thousand rupees for the week, for the groceries that will fill the kitchen, for the wages that keep the body alive. But the bridge is not merely a bridge. It is the physical embodiment of a connection that has been severed, yet continues to be targeted. Why? Because the severance is not complete. Because the thing that connects still exists, and therefore must be destroyed to make the separation absolute.

This is the dialectic of the state in its most violent form. In my notes on the East, I speak of the dream, of the spirit that does not move, that remains in the immediate, the natural, the given. But here, in Europe, I see the spirit in motion, yet a motion that is self-contradictory. The bridge is the ethical substance made concrete: it allows passage, it unites the two shores. To target it is to attack the unity itself. Why does Ukraine keep doing it? Because the unity is no longer rational. Because the bridge now serves a power that has turned the connection into a chain. The targeting is not an accident; it is the negation of a negation. The bridge was built to connect; the war breaks it to disconnect; but the breaking itself becomes a new form of connection, a shared trauma, a common focus of hatred.

I thought of the Kerch Bridge as I thought of the file at the Directorate. Both are barriers. The file bars my access to my own right, to my own identity as a resident, a citizen, a man with a name that was miswritten. The bridge bars the flow of the spirit, the movement of history. But in both cases, the barrier is not static. It is a point of tension. The file is 'gone up for orders.' It is in motion, even if it is slow. The bridge is being targeted, even if it still stands.

My earlier conviction that India stands outside world history, that it is a spirit that dreams, seems to waver when I see this. Is this the dream? Or is it the waking nightmare of a history that has not yet reached its summit? The Germanic world is supposed to be the summit, the place where freedom is realized for all. Yet here, in the summit, we see the bridge being bombed. Does this mean the summit is a lie? Or does it mean that the summit is a struggle, a constant negation of what has been achieved?

I am shaken. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, yes. But what is the ethical idea when the bridge is on fire? Is it the idea of unity, or the idea of separation? The targeting suggests that the unity has become a threat. The separation is being pursued as a good. This is not the rational state. This is the state in its moment of self-destruction, or perhaps, of self-renewal. I do not know. But I know that the bridge is not a dream. It is a thing of wood and steel, and it is being broken. And in its breaking, I see the tension that I have failed to resolve in my notes on the East. The dream is not static. The dream is the bridge being targeted. The dream is the file going up for orders. The dream is the haze clearing, only to reveal the fire behind it.

The 'dimagi' Naxal is a threat to the inner conviction, the subjective freedom that has turned against the universal.

The state seeks to save them, or to save itself from them, by aligning their minds with the actuality of the state.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East — notes on the Bastar headline

9 November 2026. Delhi.

The papers left on the verandah this morning carry three headlines. The first: Congress donations fall nearly 75%, the sharpest decline in a decade. The second: armed Naxals wiped out, need to save the country from dimagi-Naxals — the Prime Minister in Bastar. The third: Modi to celebrate Deepavali with the forces in Bastar, once a den of Maoists. I sat with them and found my old theses wobbling.

My first thesis, that India stands outside the movement of world history — that this land dreams rather than grows, that its castes are fixed like nature and its many gods belong to no state of its own making — is shaken. Not refuted. Shaken. A state that sends its Prime Minister to a forest, that announces a rebellion wiped out, that mobilizes forces to celebrate a festival in a territory it claims is being saved, is a state doing something. It names an internal enemy, it claims a country, it claims a mission. That is precisely the shape of a state as I have always described it: a universal that acts against a particular, that secures its person and property, that embodies the ethical idea. I do not yet know what to make of it. I will not pretend the shaking is over.

The second thesis, that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, is shaken too, but in a different way. The headline speaks of saving the country from dimagi-Naxals — a phrase that does double duty: it is a military claim and a moral one. The state here is not merely a neutral guardian of property; it is a save-the-country. I have always held the state as the actuality of the universal, but the universal in my Berlin was a rational, grown, constitutional order. Here the universal appears as a crusade. Is that the ethical idea, or is it a dream dressed in the language of the universal? I cannot yet say. What I can say is that the language is interesting: the state speaks in the voice of salvation, not merely administration.

What I do not know, and must mark as speculation, is what Bastar means. I have no report from inside it. The papers give me a headline and a festival. I do not know whether the forces are genuinely decisive, whether the Naxals are wiped out or merely driven, whether the festival is a real celebration or a ceremony. I will not invent a scene inside Bastar. What I can observe is the spectacle here: the Prime Minister in the forest, the Deepavali, the phrase save the country. It is a state that performs itself.

The Congress donation headline is the other half of the picture. A party's donations falling 75% is a measure of civil society — of needs, of money, of the system of interests — in decline. That is the civil society of my lecture, the system of needs preserved by law and external order. The donation figures and the Naxal headline are the two faces of the same state: the economy that feeds it and the force that saves it.

I am writing this while the household is unpaid and the file is gone up for orders. The state has not come to me; I have come to observe it. But I notice that the state is not absent here. It is present, shouting, saving, celebrating. My thesis that India is outside the movement was a thesis about a dream. The papers suggest something more like a movement, though not the movement I know. I will keep both theses alive, shaken, and return to them. I do not yet know what they will become.
